en: Advayavajra’s Works 11. *Māyānirukti*,
edited by Mahāmahopādhyāya Hara Prasad Shastri.
In *Advayavajrasaṃgraha*, GOS 1927, Baroda,
edited by the Mikkyō Seiten Kenkyūkai; in *Taishō Daigaku Sōgō Bukkyō Kenkyūjo Nenpō*.
Homage to the Buddha.

If the world is indeed devoid of intrinsic nature like an illusion, why is it that the wise, though knowing this through direct perception, still remain deluded here out of a longing for happiness? (1)
A magician creates an illusion as radiant as a blazing house;
to some it appears real, but to one who knows it, it is merely an illusion.
Those desires that come to him spontaneously, without the effort of seeking satisfaction through illusion,
he enjoys by means of illusion, since illusion is associated with everything.
Alas, tell me how there could be permanence in illusion apart from its falsity;
for since the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is unborn, the consequence of annihilation does not follow. (4)
In the case of phenomena that are indeed neither born nor ceased, one does not fall into insentience;
for a phenomenon arises from emptiness, and there is no other nature of phenomena (dharmatā) than that. 5.
For this very reason, the omniscience of the Buddha is not impaired;
through the absence of superimposition, the entire wheel of Dharma is set in motion.
Having abandoned the stretching out of the feet [of worldly conduct] and having cast aside conceptualizations such as pride,
the yogi should wander through practice, well-established by means of the yoga of non-abiding. (7)
Having obtained the essence of food and drink, he who does not practice the conduct after having clearly proclaimed it in speech is not a vessel for perfect enlightenment.
A person speaks the truth with their speech and even approves of right conduct; a person endowed with the perfection of knowledge and practice is rare to find. (9)
The earth is his bed, the directions are his garment, and alms-food is his meal;
he possesses patience regarding the unborn nature of phenomena, and his compassion flows effortlessly. || 10 ||
Those qualities which conquer people are themselves conquered by [wrong] conduct;
let this unsurpassed fruit be evident here for now. (11)
By whatever merit has been well-obtained by this virtuous mind through the unveiling of Māyā, may all beings, established in the supramundane, attain the state of non-duality. (12)
The Exposition of Māyā is completed.
Farewell.
